WAKE✳︎ is infrastructure for durable, accountable work across interchangeable
models, runtimes, and people. Research is its first application. Its name asks
us to consider what remains after an interaction ends:

> A wave describes possibilities. A wake carries the consequences of what has occurred.

This is the starting image for the **Quantum Wake Function** metaphor. The
architecture gives that image a practical expression: work can leave an
inspectable history that survives the intelligence that produced it.

## Waves and wakes

Imagine a boat crossing a quiet lake. Its wake is the disturbance left by its
passage. The boat may be gone while that disturbance continues to spread,
interact with other disturbances, and affect another boat's passage.

A wake is both evidence of the past and an influence on the future.

The distinction concerns what we are looking at: a wave's form and propagation,
or a disturbance in relation to the passage that produced it. A wake contains
waves; ordinary water waves also have causes and consequences. The opening
sentence is a metaphor, not a physical classification of waves as possibilities
and wakes as facts. Nor does a water wake preserve a complete, permanent account
of its cause. WAKE's software record supplies deliberate persistence and
provenance that water does not.

## The quantum inspiration and its limits

In quantum mechanics, a wavefunction mathematically describes a quantum state.
It provides complex probability amplitudes from which measurement probabilities
can be calculated. For discrete outcomes in the chosen measurement basis, those
probabilities are the squared magnitudes of the corresponding amplitudes. It is
not an ordinary wave in water. See IBM's
[introduction to quantum states](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/basics-of-quantum-information/single-systems/introduction)
and [measurement examples](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/utility-scale-quantum-computing/bits-gates-and-circuits).

Quantum measurement does not require a conscious observer. A measuring apparatus
can interact with a system and register an outcome without a person watching it;
see Yu and Nikolić's discussion of
[why consciousness is not required](https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.2404).

The metaphor borrows the relationship between possibilities and consequences:

> The wavefunction describes what might happen. The wake function describes how what happened shapes what can happen next.

This compresses an idea for reflection; it is not a complete account of quantum
states or measurement. **Quantum Wake Function is not an established mathematical
object or physical law.** Here, “function” names a conceptual role, not an
equation, algorithm, or software interface. WAKE does not claim to perform
quantum computation. Its operation is explained by ordinary software contracts,
not by quantum measurement. The metaphor implies no consciousness, subjective
experience, or persistent personal identity in WAKE or its models.

## How the architecture carries consequences

WAKE's concrete lifecycle is:

```text
Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt
```

| Metaphorical idea | Concrete architectural role |
| --- | --- |
| Possibility | A model receives bounded context derived from the record and produces a proposal for potential next actions. |
| Interaction | Governance deterministically evaluates the untrusted proposal against applicable policies and current governed state. |
| Consequence | Accepted transitions change governed state. A governed rejection produces a receipt without applying the rejected changes or advancing the accepted revision. |
| Wake | The durable record preserves events, decisions, receipts, provenance, and corrections. Deferrals and failures remain visible through their recorded outcomes. |
| Continuity | Subsequent work receives bounded context derived from recorded history, allowing earlier interactions to inform future proposals. |

The arrows describe the lifecycle, not a promise that every attempt makes a
transition. A provider failure before a proposal exists is recorded through the
invocation lifecycle; it does not fabricate a proposal receipt. See
[architecture and limits](architecture.md) and the [kernel contract](kernel.md)
for the actual guarantees.

For example, a rejected suggestion can help a later model understand a policy
boundary. Its receipt establishes that the rejection occurred, not that the
suggested change was made. An accepted change can establish governed work that
the next model must account for, even if that model never encountered the
original interaction.

The significant property is that consequences can persist independently of the
intelligence that produced them. A model may disappear, be replaced, or begin
again without remembering earlier work. The governed record carries forward
what was actually established within the system.

**The intelligence is replaceable. The accountable history remains.**

## Memory without model authority

The record influences future work through bounded context, not by giving a model
control over history or policy. Context may summarize or omit detail; recoverable
provenance keeps links back to the exact recorded material. A later proposal
still passes through governance. Neither a confident model nor a repeated claim
can authorize its own acceptance. See [context and retrieval](retrieval.md).

Recording evidence establishes that material was recorded with particular
provenance. It does not establish the truth of every associated claim. Even an
accepted research transition means that the proposal passed applicable rules,
not that its conclusions became unquestionable facts. Scientific support must
still be assessed, uncertainty retained, and claims open to correction.

Corrections and supersession add accountable history rather than rewriting what
happened. A later correction can change which conclusion is current while
preserving the earlier claim and why it was revised. Append-only history and
hash verification support inspection; their [audit limits](architecture.md#recovery-and-audit-limits)
still apply. Persistence alone is not proof of truth or protection against every
form of tampering.

The wake metaphor therefore belongs in WAKE's design language: it explains why
durable consequences matter. The append-only record, governed transitions, and

| Consequence | Accepted transitions change governed state. A governed rejection produces a receipt without applying the rejected changes or advancing the accepted revision. |
| Wake | The durable record preserves events, decisions, receipts, provenance, and corrections. Deferrals and failures remain visible through their recorded outcomes. |

The arrows describe the lifecycle, not a promise that every attempt makes a
transition. A provider failure before a proposal exists is recorded through the
invocation lifecycle; it does not fabricate a proposal receipt. See
[architecture and limits](architecture.md) and the [kernel contract](kernel.md)
for the actual guarantees.

For example, a rejected suggestion can help a later model understand a policy
boundary. Its receipt establishes that the rejection occurred, not that the
suggested change was made. An accepted change can establish governed work that
the next model must account for, even if that model never encountered the
original interaction.

The significant property is that consequences can persist independently of the
intelligence that produced them. A model may disappear, be replaced, or begin
again without remembering earlier work. The governed record carries forward
what was actually established within the system.

**The intelligence is replaceable. The accountable history remains.**

## Memory without model authority

The record influences future work through bounded context, not by giving a model
control over history or policy. Context may summarize or omit detail; recoverable
provenance keeps links back to the exact recorded material. A later proposal
still passes through governance. Neither a confident model nor a repeated claim
can authorize its own acceptance. See [context and retrieval](retrieval.md).

Recording evidence establishes that material was recorded with particular
provenance. It does not establish the truth of every associated claim. Even an
accepted research transition means that the proposal passed applicable rules,
not that its conclusions became unquestionable facts. Scientific support must
still be assessed, uncertainty retained, and claims open to correction.

Corrections and supersession add accountable history rather than rewriting what
happened. A later correction can change which conclusion is current while
preserving the earlier claim and why it was revised. Append-only history and
hash verification support inspection; their [audit limits](architecture.md#recovery-and-audit-limits)
still apply. Persistence alone is not proof of truth or protection against every
form of tampering.

For a first installation, follow [the simple setup guide](setup.md#1-local-docker-installation).
It covers download, Docker, credentials, inspection, research controls and recreation.
This page explains the operating contracts and retained compatibility launchers.

## Run one installation container

The current local path is one `wake` container, one web server, and twelve internal
worker processes called nodes. Three parents (`100.wake`, `200.wake`, `300.wake`)
each have three children. Nodes do not run their own web servers. The installation
controller starts, stops, and routes them; they cannot continue after it exits.
Each node retains its own governed SQLite record. The controller has no separate
writable group research database.

Prepare topics and provider settings, then build and launch from the repository:

```sh
test -f .env || cp .env.example .env
test -f research-topics.toml || cp example.research-topics.toml research-topics.toml
# Configure GEMINI_API_KEY if you intend to enable Gemini later.
# Edit your local research-topics.toml for this installation.
./scripts/wake_installation build
./scripts/wake_installation start
./scripts/wake_installation shell
wake-research --help
wake-research status
```

**Every container launch starts research stopped.** Inspection does not enable
research or Bob calls. The Console and shell are available first;
use `wake-research start` only after inspecting the installation and configuration.
The launcher neither pulls source nor switches branches. VS Code can attach to the
running `wake` container; `/workspace` is writable and the existing WAKE `.bashrc`
terminal prompt is retained.

Open `http://localhost:8080/console.html`. The container listens on port 8080; the
launcher publishes it on host port 8080 by default. Set `WAKE_PORT` before launch to
choose another host port. An iPhone on the same network uses the Mac's LAN IP,
for example `http://192.168.1.20:8080/console.html`. No DNS container is needed. The
fixed masthead selector opens the complete unified WAKE website or a node's complete
exported view. The `wake` option includes the journal, research, maps and Bob's
Blog. Its Console keeps the normal panels and adds the installation overview at
the top. Identical shared group publications appear once in the unified blog;
node contributions keep links and provenance back to their own records. A shared
publication must already be recorded before it appears; viewing the site never
ca

[... bounded source excerpt ...]

rded node result for each coordinate.
Source node, invocation and other contributions remain inspectable; multiple node
results do not count as multiple completed coordinates or averaged replications.

Paused mode
can enable and display it but never runs probes. Each ordinary answered provider
invocation scores one cell as a sidecar, including rejected research responses;
timeouts and quota deferrals leave the cell pending. The website projects recorded
progress after the cycle. No separate scheduler or extra provider call is needed.

Custom config and topics may be mounted read-only over `/app/wake.toml` and
`/app/research-topics.toml`. Mount both when changing relative topic-file paths.
The image runs as UID/GID 10001; bind-mounted data directories must be writable by
that user. Named volumes acquire the image's data-directory ownership automatically.

## Open the installation in VS Code

With the Dev Containers extension installed, add the optional editor overlay while
keeping the same Compose project name as your existing installation:

```sh
docker compose -p wake-standalone-preview -f compose.yaml -f compose.vscode.yaml up -d --build
```

The current local preview uses `wake-standalone-preview`. Substitute your own existing
project name for another installation; changing that name selects a different data volume.
This overlay keeps research paused and omits the provider credential. It mounts the
local repository at `/workspace` and a persistent, writable VS Code home at `/home/wake`.
Its optional `vscode` image target includes Git and the OpenSSH client and trusts only the `/workspace` bind
mount for Git ownership checks. The default standalone image omits editor tools.
The authority remains `/data/wake.sqlite`; the rest of the image stays read-only.

In VS Code, open the Command Palette and choose **Dev Containers: Attach to Running
Container…**, select `wake-standalone-preview-wake-1`, then open `/workspace`.
Edits there persist in your local repository. `/app` is the packaged image copy.
The overlay sets the working directory to `/workspace`, so `python -m wake.standalone`
imports that mounted source tree. The standard image runs its packaged copy from `/app`.
Confirm the actual imported path before testing. Restart the editor-mode process to
load Python changes; rebuild for dependency or packaged-image changes. Attach again after
recreation if the editor connection closes.

VS Code copies the host Git identity configuration and can forward the host SSH agent.
Use the VS Code integrated terminal for SSH Git operations; ordinary `docker exec`
sessions do not automatically receive the forwarded `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` environment.
Private keys are not mounted or baked into the image. The host agent must have your
GitHub key loaded. Normal SSH host verification still applies on the first connection.

Use both Compose files for subsequent editor-mode operations. To return to the ordinary
runtime, recreate using only `compose.yaml` and explicitly select paused or live mode.
The source mount and editor home are omitted while the same data volume is retained.

## Runtime secret file

The default Compose file passes `GEMINI_API_KEY` at runtime. Alternatively use a
Compose override (stored locally) with a Docker secret:

```yaml
services:
  wake:
    environment:
      GEMINI_API_KEY: ""
      GEMINI_API_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/gemini_api_key
    secrets:
      - gemini_api_key
secrets:
  gemini_api_key:
    file: ./secrets/gemini_api_key.txt
```

Keep the secret file outside version control, then pass both Compose files with `-f`.
The runtime refuses simultaneous nonempty environment and file credentials. Never
supply credentials as build arguments. Docker's [Compose secrets documentation](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/)
describes mounted runtime secrets.

## Stop, recreate and audit

```sh
docker compose exec wake python -m wake --data /data audit
docker compose down
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec wake python -m wake --data /data audit
```

`down` preserves the volume. **`down --volumes` deletes your local record.** Keep the

## Run one installation container

The current local path is one `wake` container, one web server, and twelve internal
worker processes called nodes. Three parents (`100.wake`, `200.wake`, `300.wake`)
each have three children. Nodes do not run their own web servers. The installation
controller starts, stops, and routes them; they cannot continue after it exits.
Each node retains its own governed SQLite record. The controller has no separate
writable group research database.

Prepare topics and provider settings, then build and launch from the repository:

```sh
test -f .env || cp .env.example .env
test -f research-topics.toml || cp example.research-topics.toml research-topics.toml
# Configure GEMINI_API_KEY if you intend to enable Gemini later.
# Edit your local research-topics.toml for this installation.
./scripts/wake_installation build
./scripts/wake_installation start
./scripts/wake_installation shell
wake-research --help
wake-research status
```

**Every container launch starts research stopped.** Inspection does not enable
research or Bob calls. The Console and shell are available first;
use `wake-research start` only after inspecting the installation and configuration.
The launcher neither pulls source nor switches branches. VS Code can attach to the
running `wake` container; `/workspace` is writable and the existing WAKE `.bashrc`
terminal prompt is retained.

Open `http://localhost:8080/console.html`. The container listens on port 8080; the
launcher publishes it on host port 8080 by default. Set `WAKE_PORT` before launch to
choose another host port. An iPhone on the same network uses the Mac's LAN IP,
for example `http://192.168.1.20:8080/console.html`. No DNS container is needed. The
fixed masthead selector opens the complete unified WAKE website or a node's complete
exported view. The `wake` option includes the journal, research, maps and Bob's
Blog. Its Console keeps the normal panels and adds the installation overview at
the top. Identical shared group publications appear once in the unified blog;
node contributions keep links and provenance back to their own records. A shared
publication must already be recorded before it appears; viewing the site never

## Open the installation in VS Code

With the Dev Containers extension installed, add the optional editor overlay while
keeping the same Compose project name as your existing installation:

```sh
docker compose -p wake-standalone-preview -f compose.yaml -f compose.vscode.yaml up -d --build
```

The current local preview uses `wake-standalone-preview`. Substitute your own existing
project name for another installation; changing that name selects a different data volume.
This overlay keeps research paused and omits the provider credential. It mounts the
local repository at `/workspace` and a persistent, writable VS Code home at `/home/wake`.
Its optional `vscode` image target includes Git and the OpenSSH client and trusts only the `/workspace` bind
mount for Git ownership checks. The default standalone image omits editor tools.
The authority remains `/data/wake.sqlite`; the rest of the image stays read-only.

In VS Code, open the Command Palette and choose **Dev Containers: Attach to Running
Container…**, select `wake-standalone-preview-wake-1`, then open `/workspace`.
Edits there persist in your local repository. `/app` is the packaged image copy.
The overlay sets the working directory to `/workspace`, so `python -m wake.standalone`
imports that mounted source tree. The standard image runs its packaged copy from `/app`.
Confirm the actual imported path before testing. Restart the editor-mode process to
load Python changes; rebuild for dependency or packaged-image changes. Attach again after
recreation if the editor connection closes.

VS Code copies the host Git identity configuration and can forward the host SSH agent.
Use the VS Code integrated terminal for SSH Git operations; ordinary `docker exec`
sessions do not automatically receive the forwarded `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` environment.
Private keys are not mounted or baked into the image. The host agent must have your
GitHub key loaded. Normal SSH host verification still applies on the first connection.

Use both Compose files for subsequent editor-mode operations. To return to the ordinary
runtime, recreate using only `compose.yaml` and explicitly select paused or live mode.
The source mount and editor home are omitted while the same data volume is retained.

## Runtime secret file

The default Compose file passes `GEMINI_API_KEY` at runtime. Alternatively use a
Compose override (stored locally) with a Docker secret:

```yaml
services:
  wake:
    environment:
      GEMINI_API_KEY: ""
      GEMINI_API_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/gemini_api_key
    secrets:
      - gemini_api_key
secrets:
  gemini_api_key:
    file: ./secrets/gemini_api_key.txt
```

Keep the secret file outside version control, then pass both Compose files with `-f`.
The runtime refuses simultaneous nonempty environment and file credentials. Never
supply credentials as build arguments. Docker's [Compose secrets documentation](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/)
describes mounted runtime secrets.
